title: Going through a discography of Sharkey recordings
summary: Looking at record listings, he identifies sessions, the Sharks of Rhythm, and which men were New York or New Orleans players.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Let me show you what I mean about Sharky having a guitar player. Hold on a second, I'll turn it off.
Meyer Weinberg. That must be New Orleans, huh? Yeah, Julian Lane, Meyer Weinberg, Dave Weinstein, tenor, Ormond Hubb. But I wasn't on there. Bill Bourgeois on bass, August Schilling on drums.
That sounds like a New Orleans band. I didn't know Ormond ever went to New York.

No, he didn't. Because Meyer Weinberg, Dave Weinstein either. He's the president of the union here. This is a misprint. These tunes we used to do in Nick's. Swing in, swing out, yes she do, no she don't. Yeah, we used to do those tunes in New York, see, at Nick's.
Here's the session you're talking about.

The next one. The band we used to call, Sharky called the band the Sharks of Rhythm while we were in New York, see? Santo and Irving Fazola, Clyde Hart, this is the record he made in New York. Frank Federico, yeah. Thurman Teague bass, and Benny Pollack, because Frank was playing with Benny Pollack and so was Thurman Teague. And this Clyde Hart is a colored boy.
Yeah, that's a good session. They have those in the public library. They have those.

This is the record I was telling you about, Mud Hole Blues, see? Moe Zutikoff, Trombone, yeah, and Joe Marsali, see? Joe Bushkin, who is quite famous today, Eddie Condon, Marty Shapiro, and George Wettling. Yeah.
Now that's when he was at Nick's he made those, but he switched the band around, right?
That's right, see, he used different fellas. Because all these tunes we were playing at Nick's, and he used the same tunes on the recording session.
What was he using Moe Zutikoff with, he had Brunis?
I can't understand that. I don't know. Well, he and Brunis were always at each other's throats. Never could get along together.
Yeah. Now here's one with Brunis, you see, and Joe Marsali, and Joe Bushkin, Eddie Condon, and Fred Whelan, and Al Seidel on drums. But that wasn't... I was playing with him at the time, 1937.
That wasn't the next band hardly at all except for Brunis, huh?

No, no, yeah, that's right. Now his one was, this was recorded in New Orleans, you see, Santo and Lester Bouchon, Jeff Riddick, Tink Morton, Monk Hazel, 1940. No, that's 49. I remember. Yeah, I remember. I remember.
